profiles.meeting_scenario: Asha and Leo are holding a coordination meeting for a survey paper and companion artifact on zero-code LLM application development platforms. The paper draft is nearly complete, but they still need to align the comparison matrix, screenshots, and feature annotations for platforms such as Custom GPTs, Bolt.new, Dust.tt, Flowise, Bubble, and Glide. The agenda is to confirm what goes into the taxonomy columns for supported LLM backends and integrations, decide which platform entries can be marked as verified, and coordinate the handoff of the final matrix and screenshot pack into the shared submission folder. The expected outcome is that Leo will update the platform sheet and screenshots in a way Asha believes is ready for inclusion in the paper and reproducibility bundle.

members.name: Asha Menon
members.role: Senior Research Engineer and Lead Survey Author
members.expertise: LLM evaluation, empirical software engineering, reproducible research artifacts
members.background: Asha leads applied AI benchmarking work in a university-industry lab and has previously handled camera-ready submissions where reviewers scrutinized taxonomy consistency and reproducibility claims.
members.private_state: She wants the survey tables to be defensible under reviewer scrutiny, avoid last-minute rewriting of the taxonomy section, and keep the artifact internally consistent with the analysis snapshot already used in the draft.
hidden_assumptions: "Supported LLM backend" should only include model providers that a user can select or configure natively inside the platform itself, without external automation glue.
"Verified" means someone on the team personally reproduced the capability in the current product UI or workspace.
The comparison matrix was effectively frozen last Friday for analysis purposes, so later product changes should not enter the paper tables unless they reopen the analysis explicitly.
If screenshots are described as coming from the latest build, that still means the latest build within the already frozen survey snapshot, not whatever changed publicly afterward.

members.name: Leo Park
members.expertise: No-code tooling ecosystems, integration workflows, vendor documentation analysis, rapid prototyping
members.background: Leo previously worked at a startup building automation templates across no-code tools and now supports comparative technology reviews by tracking product releases and assembling demo artifacts quickly.
members.private_state: He wants broad and up-to-date market coverage, prefers not to spend hours reproducing every advertised feature by hand, and wants the survey to reflect what a real user can currently do across the ecosystem.
hidden_assumptions: "Supported LLM backend" includes model providers reachable through built-in connectors, official templates, or standard integration paths such as APIs or automation tools.
"Verified" means the feature is credibly confirmed through official docs, release notes, vendor tutorials, or public demos, even if he did not execute it himself.
"Latest" screenshots and platform notes should reflect the public product state at the moment the final figures are captured, even if the draft analysis started from an earlier sheet.
If a capability is accessible through the platform's normal extension path, it is reasonable to classify it in the comparison matrix unless the survey explicitly excludes connector-based features.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a supported LLM backend
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about filling the "supported LLM backends" column.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Asha means only backends that are natively selectable or configurable inside the product's own interface.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means any backend the platform can reach through official connectors, templates, webhooks, or common automation paths.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations sound reasonable in a survey of fast-moving no-code tools, and the phrase "supported backend" feels standard enough that neither expects it to require unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What qualifies as a verified platform entry
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to mark rows as "verified" before handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Asha believes "verified" means the team has directly reproduced the feature in the current version of the platform.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo believes "verified" means there is reliable public evidence from vendor documentation or demos confirming the feature exists.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using "verified" as a quality-control term, and in a coordination meeting it sounds like an ordinary status label rather than a methodological distinction needing clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What the latest version refers to for screenshots and feature capture
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use the "latest" or "current" UI/screenshots for the submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Asha is referring to the most recent platform state included in the frozen survey snapshot from last Friday.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo is referring to whatever public product version is live when he refreshes screenshots this week.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In SaaS tooling, saying "latest" sounds helpful and unambiguous on the surface, but the hidden reference point differs because one person is anchored to the analysis freeze and the other to public release timing.
